newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Austria urges EU to label gene foods for consumers.
newsitem.headline: Austria urges EU to label gene foods for consumers.

text.p: Consumers must be clearly informed so that they can choose whether or not to buy genetically modified food, Austrian Farm Minister Wilhelm Molterer said on Tuesday.

Food safety is a sensitive issue in Austria where last week over 1.2 million people, or more than one in four voters, signed a petition calling for a ban on the release of genetically modified organisms or GMOs into food or the environment.
"All foods containing GMOs must be labelled," Molterer told Reuters in an interview. "It must be made clear to consumers what's in food so that they can make a rational choice."

Seeds and animal feed, as well as food for human consumption, must be labelled if they contain GMOs, added Molterer, who earlier had pressed European Union farm ministers on the urgent need for clear EU rules.
Northern member states had informally expressed strong support for Austria's demand, he said, adding that the European Commission was working hard on drafting proposals.
In June, EU Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard is due to propose a tightening of rules on the use of GMOs released into the environment.

The EU's Austrian Farm Commissioner, Franz Fischler, is drawing up radical plans to segregate and label all gene-modified animal feed, irrespective of the percentage of GMOs it contained. Seeds would also have to be labelled.

On Tuesday, Fischler told farm ministers that special rules were needed for genetically modified products approved by the EU and on the market. The rules would target gene-modified soybeans made by Monsanto and a maize strain engineered by Ciba Geigy.
Austria, which sees itself as a leader on environmental issues, in January defied the EU and banned the import of the maize from the United States saying it posed a health risk.
Austrian evidence in support of its claim is being examined by EU scientific committees.

"We believe we have a very good scientific basis for the import ban," said Molterer, noting that the European Parliament this month called for the suspension of all genetically modified maize pending further health and safety tests.
Other EU countries shared Austria's view, he noted. Luxembourg has banned imports of the maize viariety, while France and Italy have stopped farmers from growing it.
